cf.title: Use maintenance_io_concurrency for parallel index builds

input.subject: [PATCH] Use maintenance_io_concurrency for parallel index builds

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: these scans do maintenance work and reuse an existing flag and setting. Two fixable points remain. standards-compat-1 asks why a change in prefetch depth belongs in stable branches, and which ones. maintenance-fit-2 asks for a rule on which scans pass SO_MAINTENANCE and why the concurrent validation scan is left out. A committer can settle both, most likely by applying to master only.

brief.title: Use maintenance_io_concurrency for index builds and table rewrites
brief.problem: Heap scans in index builds and table rewrites take their read stream prefetch depth from effective_io_concurrency, a query setting, so maintenance_io_concurrency has no effect on them. This affects administrators who tune maintenance I/O separately. The CommitFest entry tags it as a bugfix targeting stable branches.
brief.proposed_design: The patch passes the maintenance context (SO_MAINTENANCE) through existing scan flags so these read streams use maintenance_io_concurrency, including tablespace overrides. Serial builds call table_beginscan_common() directly instead of changing the table AM API. v4 covers serial and parallel B-tree, GIN and BRIN builds, BRIN range summarization, and the sequential heap scan of VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and REPACK.
user_visible_surface: Behaviour change: maintenance_io_concurrency (and its tablespace override) now controls heap prefetch in create index, BRIN summarization, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and REPACK.
src/include/access/tableam.h changes, which table AM extensions may see; the commit message says interfaces are preserved.
author_claims: Parallel B-tree, GIN and BRIN builds use effective_io_concurrency because they do not pass READ_STREAM_MAINTENANCE.
The fix keeps existing scan options and interfaces unchanged.
The heap validation scan of concurrent index creation stays unchanged on purpose.
Yuhang Qiu agrees the problem is real and says the fix looks good.
brief.thread_state: Yuhang Qiu reviewed v1 and suggested the serial-path approach, which v3 adopted. Nobody has replied to v4, which added the VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and REPACK scans.
unclear: The patch shows no benchmark of the effect on build or rewrite time.
The thread does not justify backpatching a change that alters I/O behaviour in stable branches, nor say which branches.
The patch does not say why the concurrent index validation scan stays on effective_io_concurrency.
The patch has no documentation change, so maintenance_io_concurrency docs may not list these operations.
The thread does not say whether non-heap table AMs need to honour the flag.

objections.title: Backpatching changes prefetch depth for existing installations on a minor upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA raised effective_io_concurrency for fast storage and left maintenance_io_concurrency at its default. After a minor upgrade, create index, VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER prefetch less, and nightly maintenance windows run longer. The DBA learns of it only when jobs overrun, with no release note telling them which setting to change.
objections.argument: The CommitFest entry targets "stable", but none of the five messages argues for a backpatch or says which branches. The patch moves which setting controls I/O for common maintenance commands, so tuned systems see a change they did not ask for in a minor release. A committer would likely treat this as a master-only behaviour change unless the docs already promise the new behaviour. REPACK also appears in v4, so a backpatched version would differ by branch and still needs to be defined.
objections.author_must_show: Which branches should get this, and why is a changed I/O setting for create index and VACUUM FULL acceptable in a minor release for already tuned systems?

critic.reasoning: The CommitFest entry targets stable, but no message names branches or argues for a backpatch. The scenario is concrete: a site that raised only effective_io_concurrency gets shallower prefetch for create index and VACUUM FULL after a minor upgrade.

objections.title: No stated rule for which scans count as maintenance
objections.failure_scenario: A developer later adds a heap scan to a maintenance command, or a table AM implements index_build_range_scan, without passing SO_MAINTENANCE. That scan silently uses effective_io_concurrency, and nothing fails. Users see one command follow two settings and report it as a new bug.
objections.argument: Coverage is opt-in per call site. v4 shows this, because the copy_for_cluster scan was found weeks after v3 (message #5). Create index concurrently would also still mix two settings in one command, since the validation scan is left unchanged without a stated reason. A committer would likely ask for a written rule, in the docs or near the flag, that says which scans must pass it.
objections.author_must_show: What rule decides which scans must pass SO_MAINTENANCE, and why does the concurrent index validation scan fall outside it?

critic.reasoning: Per-call-site opt-in copies how READ_STREAM_MAINTENANCE already works, so that part is not this patch's fault. The commit message still gives no reason for leaving the concurrent validation scan unchanged, and message #5 shows a scan was missed without a stated rule.

refuted.title: Documented contract of maintenance_io_concurrency is not updated or made consistent
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator tunes maintenance_io_concurrency to speed up create index concurrently. The initial build uses the new value, but the validation scan still follows effective_io_concurrency. The documentation does not say which phases follow which setting, so they cannot predict or tune the whole command.
refuted.argument: The patch touches no documentation, so the docs do not list which commands now follow maintenance_io_concurrency and which do not. The commit message leaves the concurrent validation scan unchanged on purpose but gives no reason. That means one command uses two settings. Changing what a GUC controls normally comes with a documentation change that states the new scope.
refuted.author_must_show: What rule decides which scans follow maintenance_io_concurrency, why does the concurrent validation scan fall outside it, and where will the documentation state this?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which asks the same question about the rule and the concurrent validation scan and has thread evidence from message #5. The remaining part is the missing documentation change, which the rubric puts out of scope at level 4.

refuted.title: Backpatching changes index build and rewrite I/O in minor releases
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator on fast storage raised effective_io_concurrency and left maintenance_io_concurrency at its default. After a minor upgrade, their create index and VACUUM FULL runs prefetch less and take longer. They find out when a maintenance window overruns, with no release note that they would read as a tuning change.
refuted.argument: The CommitFest entry targets stable branches and is tagged Bugfix. The thread does not say which branches, and no message argues that the current behaviour is a bug rather than undocumented behaviour that sites may have tuned around. The patch has no benchmark, so neither the gain nor the regression for such sites is measured. A committer would likely accept this for master and ask for a separate case for backpatching.
refuted.author_must_show: Which stable branches should get this, and why is changing their maintenance I/O depth in a minor release safer than leaving it for the next major release?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which has the same scenario and the same question and also covers the per-branch difference for REPACK.

refuted.title: No user report to justify changing I/O behaviour in stable branches
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator raised effective_io_concurrency for fast storage and left maintenance_io_concurrency at a lower value. After a minor release, create index, VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER read the heap with shallower prefetch. The administrator finds out when a scheduled rebuild runs longer than its maintenance window.
refuted.argument: The CommitFest entry targets stable and tags the patch as a bugfix, but the thread contains no field report, no -bugs or -general thread, and no measurement of the effect. The only support for the change is message #3, which agrees the problem is real. That is a reasonable case for master, where the behaviour change is announced in release notes. In a minor release, the users who gain are those who tuned maintenance_io_concurrency and expected it to apply, while the users who lose are those whose index builds silently get slower.
refuted.author_must_show: Which users have reported slow or misbehaving index builds or rewrites because of this, and why should it not wait for the next major release?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1: the objection accepts the change for master and its failure scenario is the same backpatch regression. The missing field report adds no separate failure beyond the backpatch question.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch changes src/include/access/tableam.h, which out-of-tree table AMs compile against, and the entry targets stable branches.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: No new GUC, but maintenance_io_concurrency gains control of create index, BRIN summarization, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and REPACK heap scans.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CommitFest entry is tagged Bugfix with target version stable, and REPACK does not exist in all branches.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: Each maintenance scan must pass SO_MAINTENANCE itself, and nothing fails when a new call site omits it.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes the prefetch depth of heap scans in index builds and table rewrites, with no benchmark shown.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which stable branches should get this change, and why is a different prefetch depth for create index and VACUUM FULL acceptable in a minor release?
What rule decides which scans must pass SO_MAINTENANCE, and why does the heap validation scan of concurrent index creation fall outside it?
Does the tableam.h change keep struct layout and flag values compatible for table AM extensions compiled against current stable branches?
What is the measured effect on create index and VACUUM FULL time when maintenance_io_concurrency and effective_io_concurrency differ?
Are non-heap table AMs expected to honour SO_MAINTENANCE in their own index build and rewrite scans?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the read stream code and the table AM scan interface would have to own it; no committer has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a change in maintenance I/O depth on tuned systems, for tableam.h compatibility if backpatched, and for later reports of scans that still use effective_io_concurrency.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted four versions in the thread and adopted the reviewer's serial-path suggestion in v3, which suggests continued engagement.

priority.reason: The patch is 5.7 KB, reuses an existing flag and setting, and helps administrators who tune maintenance I/O separately. The open points are the backpatch scope and a stated rule for which scans pass the flag.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can confirm that the tableam.h change is ABI-compatible on stable branches or that every maintenance heap scan now passes the flag.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Insert Prefetching
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an index AM callback amprefetch, implemented for btree, that walks the inner pages of each index and prefetches the target leaf page before index tuples are inserted. The executor calls it for all indexes, and for whole COPY batches, behind a GUC enable_insert_prefetch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected that the patch duplicates the btree descent code and its runtime work, and only helps index insertion. He suggested a general async execution model, where aminsert() returns a future that can wait on I/O. The author found the idea interesting but raised open questions about control flow and concurrency. The patch then stopped applying, and no new version appears before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't like this approach. It duplicates the tree-descend code, and it
also duplicates the work of descending the tree at runtime.

precedents_retrieved.title: Incremental Materialized View Maintenance
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add incremental materialized views (CREATE INCREMENTAL MATERIALIZED VIEW) that Postgres keeps current in the same transaction as base table changes, using AFTER triggers and transition tables. The patch computes deltas from the view definition and applies them to the view, with support for joins, some built-in aggregates, EXISTS subqueries and outer joins.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier marked the entry Returned with Feedback after a month with no update. In July 2022 huyajun had reported bugs: a deadlock between TRUNCATE and concurrent INSERT, wrong counts after concurrent DELETEs, crashes on mismatched column lists, and an unwanted unique index on cross joins. The author said he was still working on them. Paquier also noted little design discussion in three years, and Greg Stark had earlier called the patch hard to review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There has been some feedback sent lately and no update
for one month, so I am marking it as RwF for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: prefetching for nestloop / indexscan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an ExecPrefetch executor callback so that a nested loop reads a batch of outer rows and asks a parameterized inner index scan to prefetch the matching heap pages. It is a small proof of concept limited to nestloop with an inner index scan, controlled by a new enable_nestloop_prefetch setting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry because the patch was a quick experiment and he had no time to keep working on it. Before that, Andres Freund questioned the extra executor tree traversals and suggested passing multiple values down in one parameter, possibly as one ScalarArrayOps index scan. Peter Geoghegan supported that direction. The author agreed it looks like block nested loop join, which moves the work away from this design, and his cached-data benchmark showed about a 30% regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But
the patch was just a quick & dirty experiment, I don't have time to work
on this right now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix search_path for maintenance commands
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch sets search_path to "pg_catalog, pg_temp" while ANALYZE, CLUSTER, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, REINDEX, VACUUM and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW run as the table owner. This makes the commands behave the same for every caller and keeps a role with the MAINTAIN privilege from using search_path to gain the table owner's privileges.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Jeff Davis withdrew the patch after a reviewer reported that it no longer applied to HEAD, saying it was not yet clear this was the right change. He had already noted that it forces search_path in maintenance commands but not in other contexts, and that his broader proposals to fix search_path for functions got little agreement. Earlier concerns about breaking functions that depend on search_path were raised in messages not shown. Nathan Bossart supported committing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I am withdrawing this patch from the CF until it's more clear that this is what we really want to do.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow tuple visibility checks without hint-bit maintenance
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds HeapTupleSatisfiesVisibilityNoHints() and HeapTupleSatisfiesUpdateNoHints(), which return the normal visibility verdict without setting hint bits on the buffer. It targets table AMs that store heap-format tuples on pages logged through generic WAL, where an unlogged hint-bit write changes the page that a later generic WAL delta is computed against.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund asked why Postgres should support such an AM, since the patch did not explain its purpose. He also said the extra branches in performance-critical visibility code can slow it down, and that code with no in-tree users tends to bit-rot. The author replied that these comments led him to revisit the design, and he withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Why do we care about such an AM? What's the point of all of this?

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow tuple visibility checks without hint-bit, maintenance
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds HeapTupleSatisfiesVisibilityNoHints() and HeapTupleSatisfiesUpdateNoHints(), which return the normal visibility verdict without writing hint bits to the page. It targets table AMs that store heap-format tuples on pages logged with generic WAL, where an unlogged hint-bit write changes the before-image of the next delta.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why the author withdrew it. The entry was withdrawn the day after posting, and shihao zhong withdrew a duplicate entry (7215) in favor of 7212, which may be this record. Andres Freund objected that the patch has no in-tree user and so may bit-rot, that it adds branches to performance-critical code, and that it does not explain why such an AM matters. shihao zhong questioned the corruption claim and suggested the effect may only be a wal_consistency_checking failure.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also, having code that has no users in tree also makes it more likely to bit-rot.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prefetch the next tuple's memory during seqscans
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_prefetch_mem() macro and uses it in heapam.c to prefetch the next tuple's memory during page-mode sequential scans. Tuples sit in reverse order on the heap page, and the author expected CPU hardware prefetchers to miss this backward access pattern.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch. After the heapgettup()/heapgettup_pagemode refactor, he could no longer show the earlier seqscan speedup, and Apple M1 and Power8 tests showed no gain. He also came to believe that modern hardware prefetchers detect backward access patterns, and he wants to benchmark this before resubmitting.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem I'm facing is that after Melanie's recent
refactor work done around heapgettup() [1], I can no longer get the
same speedup as before with the pg_prefetch_mem().

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid smgrimmedsync() during index build and add unbuffered IO API
precedents_retrieved.summary: Index builds that write outside shared buffers would stop calling smgrimmedsync() at the end and register fsync requests with the checkpointer instead, falling back to an immediate sync only if the redo pointer moved during the build. A new unbuffered IO API (unbuffered_prep/extend/write/finish) would wrap this logic, WAL-logging and checksums for nbtree and other access methods.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because it waited on the author after review. Andres Freund's March 2022 review asked for API changes, including flag arguments, renamed parameters and functions, documentation and a README update. Heikki Linnakangas then objected that nbtsort.c still chooses between the buffer manager and the new API itself, so every index AM would have to copy that logic, and he proposed a bulk-write API that hides the choice. No new version followed in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm surprised by all the changes in nbtsort.c to choose between using
the buffer manager or the new API. I would've expected the new API to
abstract that away.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes in HOT handling of BRIN indexes
Reverted commit(s): Ignore BRIN indexes when checking for HOT udpates; Move test for BRIN HOT behavior to stats.sql
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 5753d4ee32 and fe60b67250 that modified HOT to
ignore BRIN indexes. The commit message for 5753d4ee32 claims that:

    When determining whether an index update may be skipped by using
    HOT, we can ignore attributes indexed only by BRIN indexes. There
    are no index pointers to individual tuples in BRIN, and the page
    range summary will be updated anyway as it relies on visibility
    info.

This is partially incorrect - it's true BRIN indexes don't point to
individual tuples, so HOT chains are not an issue, but the visibitlity
info is not sufficient to keep the index up to date. This can easily
result in corrupted indexes, as demonstrated in the hackers thread.

This does not mean relaxing the HOT restrictions for BRIN is a lost
cause, but it needs to handle the two aspects (allowing HOT chains and
updating the page range summaries) as separate. But that requires a
major changes, and it's too late for that in the current dev cycle.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
Reverted commit(s): VACUUM: ignore indexing operations with CONCURRENTLY
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

roaster_notes.note: The precedent search found no earlier proposal with the same or a similar idea, and no thread message points to an earlier discussion. Without a prior rejection reason to apply, the prior-attempts angle has no objection to raise.
Both objections concern scope and release policy. Moving these scans to maintenance_io_concurrency looks consistent with what the setting is meant for.

The patch changes only the prefetch depth of read streams in index builds and table rewrites. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog change, wire protocol message or cross-node state, so standbys, subscribers and pg_upgrade are unaffected. The nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping invariant does not apply. The one open point is the tableam.h change in a stable-branch target: a committer would likely ask whether the struct and flag layout stay ABI-compatible for out-of-tree table AMs, which cannot be checked without the code.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It only changes which existing setting, effective_io_concurrency or maintenance_io_concurrency, sets the prefetch depth for scans the user is already allowed to run; both settings are user-settable today with the same tablespace overrides, so nothing new becomes visible or reachable.
The core idea is small and reuses an existing mechanism, so I see no fit or hot-path objection. The nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping invariant does not apply, because the patch changes only prefetch depth.

The proposal adds no new mechanism. It makes the existing maintenance_io_concurrency and READ_STREAM_MAINTENANCE path cover more maintenance scans. Running `set effective_io_concurrency` before create index or VACUUM FULL gets the same effect, but that works around the mismatch rather than offering a competing feature, so no already-exists objection applies.
The change itself fits the documented purpose of maintenance_io_concurrency and costs little for non-users. A master-only version would draw no demand objection from this angle.
